# Business payroll handoff: worked definition exercise

**Illustrative thought experiment.** This fictional organization, its agreements, payment amounts, deadlines, configurations and records exist only to test the draft. No actual payroll, bank transaction, employment rule or measured service performance is asserted. The amounts are fictional accounting units; all clock times in this scenario are UTC.

Read with [requirements](../standard/ontology/concepts/requirement.md), [process](../standard/ontology/concepts/process.md), [system and implementation](../standard/ontology/concepts/system.md), [composition](../standard/mereology/composition-and-boundaries.md), and [assessment](../standard/assessment/requirement-and-need-fulfillment.md).

## Need, requirements and contribution

The organization needs its agreed compensation to reach the intended recipients correctly and predictably. Its four recipients also need usable payment, not merely a file saying it was submitted.

The example's payroll lead adopts requirement revision A:

| Label | Statement and criterion | Required conditions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| B1 | By Friday 17:00 in each applicable cycle, recipients A, B, C and D must each have the agreed amount credited to their nominated account: 100, 200, 300 and 400 units respectively. All four must be correct and on time. | The four approved domestic-account payments in this scenario, funded and submitted under the stipulated arrangement. A rejected payment is a case requiring response within this obligation, not grounds for retrospectively excluding its recipient. Other payment routes are outside the example's declared scope. |
| B2 | Submit a file containing the four approved payment instructions, matching the approved register and accepted by the receiving bank's file interface, by Wednesday 12:00. | Same cycle; preparation, approval and submission subprocess. Interface acceptance means receipt and file validation, not account credit. |

B2 is intended to contribute to B1 by providing time for settlement and correction. Its rationale assumes accurate account information, usable funding and successful downstream handling. B2 alone does not establish B1. B1 is high-level relative to file preparation, submission and payment-resolution requirements, even after those responsibilities have been allocated.

Successful credit is a stronger indicator of the stated payment need than submission. The broader claim that compensation is predictable over time still requires more than one cycle, and may involve recipient experience outside these criteria. This example does not resolve the owner's general assumption that sufficient, correctly realized requirements will meet a need.

## Boundary, structure and implementation

The internal payroll system contains the approved register, preparation and approval activities, submission tooling, reconciliation information and assigned people. The bank is an external dependency of this internal system. The B1 assessment covers the joint payment arrangement through recipient credit, so stopping at the internal boundary would answer a different question.

Configuration A is a hypothetical implemented register, file exporter, bank connection and manual reconciliation routine. Its existence does not establish verified readiness or successful payment. A file exporter can satisfy its local function while the combined arrangement fails B1.

The structure connects the register to four instructions, an approved batch to a submission receipt, and individual payments to their reconciliation records. Dependence on the bank does not make the bank an owned internal component. B1 depends on the interaction of preparation, submission, bank processing and exception response; component scores cannot be added to infer the joint result.

## Responsibilities and intended process

| Role | Example-specific responsibility and authority |
| --- | --- |
| Payroll operator | Prepare, submit and reconcile the batch; identify missing or failed payments and escalate. |
| Payroll lead | Maintain the process and remain accountable for unresolved payments through resolution; coordinate with the bank and recipients. |
| Finance approver | Authorize the initial batch and corrected payment instructions. Approval does not establish settlement. |
| Bank | Process accepted instructions and return payment-level outcomes under the scenario's agreement. |
| Payroll lead as assessor | Compare records with B1/B2 and decide whether to close internal reconciliation. The same person may hold several roles; their remits remain distinct. |

The intended process prepares and approves instructions, submits the file, reconciles individual credits, responds to rejections and missing results, and closes reconciliation only when each payment has a known disposition. Closing with a known late payment preserves its missed-deadline assessment; closing with a failed payment does not declare the obligation discharged.

| State subject | Trigger and condition | Result and responsible response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Submission execution | Finance approval and available funded instructions | Operator submits; interface receipt ends submission when B2's conditions hold. |
| Individual payment | Bank reports credit | Credited; operator checks recipient, amount and time. |
| Individual payment | Bank rejects an instruction | Rejected, independently of internal approval; payroll lead owns response, operator investigates, finance approver authorizes a correction. |
| Reconciliation record | Expected response absent | Outcome unknown in this record; operator investigates. This is not evidence that the payment itself failed. |
| Corrective payment | Correction approved and sent | Awaiting result until payment-level evidence arrives. Sending a correction does not close the payment obligation. |

A rejection has an anticipated response in the description while remaining outside normal successful payment progression. This tests the exception distinction without redefining every planned alternative as an exception. Role delegation and shared authority beyond this simple arrangement remain unresolved elsewhere.

## Cycle A: stipulated execution and evidence

The examined scope is one cycle, Configuration A and requirement revision A. The fictional records are: an approved four-instruction register; the submitted four-instruction file and a recorded comparison establishing that its recipients, account identifiers and amounts match that register; a Wednesday 11:00 file-acceptance receipt; payment records showing A and B credited correctly by Friday 16:00; a Friday 15:00 rejection for C; and no payment-level result for D by assessment time. The scenario stipulates that C remained uncredited at the deadline. Missing evidence for D does not stipulate its actual payment state.

At Friday 17:15, the payroll lead assesses these scenario inputs:

| Question | Bounded conclusion |
| --- | --- |
| Was submission completed? | Yes. The described submission subprocess produced its accepted file receipt before the cutoff. |
| Was B2 fulfilled? | Yes for this cycle, given the stipulated approved instructions and receipt. |
| Was B1 fulfilled? | No. C was not credited on time, which defeats the all-four criterion. D's outcome remains unknown; that uncertainty does not erase C's known failure. |
| What partial achievement is established? | Two of four required payments are known correct and on time, one is known not on time, and one is unknown. Do not turn the unknown into a failure or describe 2/4 as the arrangement's reliability or capability. |
| What happened to acceptance and responsibility? | Bank file acceptance concerns B2's handoff. The payroll lead keeps payment resolution open; the operator's submission completion does not end the lead's continuing responsibility. |
| Was the need met? | This cycle does not meet the stated all-recipient payment need. The records say little about long-term predictability or wider recipient experience. |

Only this cycle is examined. Network interruption, duplicate delivery, account changes and subsequent cycles remain untested; absence of observations is not absence of those risks or proof of capability under them. No confidence score or overall fulfillment percentage is inferred.

## Recovery, costs and review

In a separate stipulated recovery, C receives a corrected payment on Monday. The current unpaid balance for C is resolved, while B1's Friday deadline remains missed. This shows why present state and assessment over a historical interval must remain distinguishable. D still requires investigation unless new evidence establishes its disposition.

Manual reconciliation and correction consume staff time and may incur fees in the fictional arrangement. Faster submission or lower preparation cost can be a poor trade if failures remain unnoticed. No new cost requirement is inferred merely because this tradeoff is relevant.

A changed bank interface, recipient register, process, configuration or deadline changes the applicability of prior conclusions. A later authorized requirement change must not silently overwrite the criterion used to assess Cycle A.

The exercise tests completion versus outcome, normal flow versus anticipated exception, partial achievement with a known unmet criterion, unknown evidence, external dependencies and continuing responsibility. It leaves the general aggregation and minimum-recording rules open. The [paired-example review](../../source-locators.md#source-9e133881b6d48838) records the combined findings and task links.
